headline: East end on the 4:52 ebb: bass on the eel bite, blues run the bait through daylight
subhead: The full-moon push did exactly what we said it would — now the tide's easing toward neap and the program shifts to full dark.
body_markdown:
4:52 AM. That's when the ebb really got moving at the Sandwich side this week, and if you weren't rigged and drifting an eel past the Bourne Bridge piling seam by 4:30, you missed the best twenty minutes of your night. I've fished this ditch long enough to know the current doesn't care what time your alarm says — it cares what the moon says, and right now we're still riding the tail of the full moon push, with tide stages running strong and current speeds up around 4 to 4.5 knots on the peak ebb at the east end. That's canal-standard big-water speed, the kind that pins bait against the rip line off Scusset and makes big bass stop thinking and start eating.

We flagged this coming last week — said the building full-moon tide would sharpen the current push and open up the feeding windows, and that's exactly what's played out. The bite hasn't been all-day easy, but the tide-change windows have been money. East end, working the last hour of the ebb into the top of the slack, guys throwing 9-inch swimming plugs — Gags, Beachmasters, the darker patterns — through the seam where the rip meets the flat water off Scusset Beach have connected on bass in the 28 to 36-inch range after dark. Daytime, that same stretch is bluefish water. Blues are thriving in this warm surface layer that's pushing bass down and out — mid-70s water at the surface, maybe kissing 80 in the shallows on a hot afternoon, and that's blue heaven. Diamond jigs and Ava 27s worked through the froth when the bait schools push through on the tide have been good for quick limits, fish mostly in the 3 to 6 pound class, some bigger mixed in when a bunker school gets pinned against the rocks.

West end tells a different story right now. The current seams off Mashnee Island and up into the mouth by Hog Island are holding fish, but you have to work the stages right — the top third of the flood, before the current really builds, has been the window. Bucktails, half-ounce to an ounce depending on how much water's moving, bounced along bottom through the seam where the deeper channel water meets the shallower flat off Mashnee, have picked at fluke — nothing spectacular, mostly 15 to 18 inches with a keeper mixed in here and there, but steady enough to make it worth a drift if bass aren't cooperating. Phinneys Harbor has stayed quieter than I'd like this week — warm, still water in there, and without a hard tide push flushing bait through, it's been mostly small blues and the occasional schoolie bass chasing silversides at first light.

Here's the truth on the bass right now: the big fish are still here, but they've gone strictly nocturnal on us. That warm surface water — I'm talking mid-70s to near 80 from the Bay side clear through Buzzards Bay — has pushed the quality fish off the shallow structure during daylight and onto the current-swept holes and the deeper edges, where they'll only really commit to feeding on the strongest tide stages, dawn, dusk, or full dark. That's why the 4:52 ebb mattered this week, and why the corresponding evening ebb — running close to 5:15 PM by my watch — has been the other reliable window. Eels fished dead-drift on a fish-finder rig, or live-lined and let to swim naturally through the rip, have out-produced everything else after dark. If you're bucktailing in daylight expecting the same results you got in June, you're going to be disappointed — the fish simply aren't up shallow chasing plastic at 2 in the afternoon anymore.

Now, the tide's about to ease. We're coming off the full-moon peak and sliding toward neap over the next several days, current speeds dropping a bit on both ends. That usually means the bite windows get shorter and pickier — the fish won't be forced to feed as hard, so you need to be exactly where the bait is exactly when the current turns. I'd focus the next week on the last two hours of the night ebb at the east end and the top of the flood at the west end, because those are the stages that'll still be moving enough water to concentrate bait even as the overall push softens.

One more thing worth watching: with squid starting to show around the Rhode Island and Nantucket Sound edges and inshore temps holding in a range that's finally right for it, I wouldn't be shocked to hear the first bonito or false albacore scout report out of the Buzzards Bay corridor within the next week or two — that's a Woods Hole and Wings Neck story more than a straight canal story, but it's close enough to our water that I'll be watching for it. For now, though, the canal's still a bass-and-blues program, tide-driven like always, and that's not changing anytime soon. If I had one night to fish this week, I'd take the late ebb at Scusset with a black eel and patience, and I'd have a bucktail rigged as backup for when the blues show up and ruin the eel supply.
